title: An audience of one
hookLine: enough are few, enough is one, enough is none

cards: A post gets four likes and you feel faintly foolish for sharing it. A song you worked on for months gets a hundred plays. A talk you prepared gets a half-empty room.
There's a number under nearly everything we make now. Seneca didn't have the number, but he knew the itch.
Right after warning Lucilius about the crowd, he ends his seventh letter with three small sayings about how big an audience really needs to be.

teach.b: Lucilius might object: then what did I learn all this for, if no one will hear it? Seneca's first answer: you learned it for yourself. Then he gives three sayings, like three small gifts.

teach.h: DEMOCRITUS: ONE IS A WHOLE PEOPLE.
teach.b: First, Democritus, the old philosopher of atoms: one person counts as much as a whole people to me, and a whole people as much as one. The size of the audience doesn't change the worth of the work.
Second, a craftsman, though Seneca says it's uncertain who. Asked why he took such pains over an art very few would ever appreciate, he answered: a few are enough for me. One is enough.

teach.h: A FEW, ONE, EVEN NONE IS ENOUGH.
teach.b: None is enough. The work was worth doing well for its own sake.
Third, Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, writing to a friend who studied with him: I say this not for the many, but for you; we are each a big enough audience for the other.
Seneca's point, gathering all three: don't let the pleasure of being praised by many pull you back into the crowd.
Most of the good in the world is done for an audience of one: a meal for a sick friend, a letter, a careful repair, a child's question answered properly. Nobody counts those. They count anyway.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism try to do their work well regardless of how many will see it, treating a single person, or no one, as audience enough.

games.q: you're a craftsman pouring months into work very few people will ever appreciate. someone asks why you bother. what do you say?
o: a few are enough for me; one is enough; none is enough.
games.why: that's the answer Seneca passes on: the work was worth doing well even with no audience at all.

practice: Picture one person who will benefit from something you do today: a coworker, a parent, a kid with homework, a patient, a neighbor.
See their face, and picture doing that one thing really well, as if they were the whole audience, because they are. Let that be enough.
